title: Replying to @landonhudsonofficial #broadway #musicaltheatre #inthehei...
transcript: Does in the Heights have an anticlimactic ending? Interesting question. And actually, preparing for this video made me think about some things in the show that I'd never really thought about before. I believe Lin-Manuel joked about this once. I had trouble finding the exact quote, but I think I remember him saying something like, “I wrote a whole show once about a guy who's gonna go on vacation and then doesn't.” And I get it. There's very few stories that end with the main character going, “eh, never mind.” If I were to criticize the ending, I would call it more rushed than anything else. It does sort of feel like he turns on a dime, sings a little bit about how he's staying home, and then that's just the end of the show. But then again, *does* he turn on a dime? I would argue the song Champagne very much lays the groundwork for the ending, planting the idea in Usnavi's head that he should stay. Kind of funny, I guess, that having the woman of your dreams beg you to stay would probably be enough for most people, but for Usnavi, it takes seeing a mural painted by a guy he hates. But the central question of the show is essentially the meaning of home: Is it where your cultural heritage originated, or is it where you built your community? And from the moment we meet Usnavi, he's convinced himself that his problems will be solved by returning to his roots. But seeing the mural makes him realize that Washington Heights was his home all along. But this raised a different question for me that I'd never thought that hard about before: Why, specifically, did the mural have this effect on him when Abuela Claudia was encouraging him to leave, she was part of the plan to go with him. And even that itself is a little counterintuitive, given that she was a pillar of this community. According to normal narrative conventions, you would kind of expect the wise old grandma character to align with the final lesson of the show. But I think it's a testament to the fact that Abuela Claudia is not just a wise old grandma character. She's her own character with her own struggles. In the song, Paciencia y Fe we see that she's wrestling with a similar question, but informed by her own experiences. One of my favorite lyrics in the entire show is this absolute gut punch of a line where she says to her mother, “what do you do when your dreams come true?” “I've spent my life inheriting dreams from you.” For Claudia, the American dream was more her mother's dream. And even here at the end of her life, she never totally reckoned with her own sense of place and identity. Maybe she plans to leave with Usnavi because there's this sense that as wise and as caring as she is, maybe she herself doesn't know how important she is to the rest of this community. And it's Usnavi's role to realize in the final moments of the show that he needs, and in fact, wants to pick up where she left off and be there for the community that was always there for him. All that to say, while I agree that the execution of the ending is a little rushed, a little jarring, I think it makes complete narrative and thematic sense and is gorgeous.
